title: Central Washington's Congressional Seat, Now Open - NewsRadio 560 KPQ
content: Congressman Dan Newhouse is retiring from his 4th District seat in central Washington, and Republican Amanda McKinney and Democrat John Duresky emerged from a crowded primary field of candidates to advance to the November ballot. Amanda McKinney is a Yakima County Commissioner with roles on the Washington state and national associations of counties. McKinney is a small business owner with 20 years of experience in mortgage banking. John Duresky has no previous elected experience but is retired Air Force, serving 24 years as a cyberspace officer, working with the NSA, the CIA, and at Hanford, according to his candidate profile. TownSquare Media (TSM) posed several questions to both candidates but only received a response from McKinney. TSM; Please describe three major pillars of your campaign. What should voters consider about your candidacy for this seat? My campaign is built on three priorities: protecting water and agriculture, lowering costs and supporting a strong local economy, and keeping decisions close to the communities they affect. Water is essential to Central Washington’s farms, families, and future growth. I will work to protect existing water rights and support the infrastructure our communities need. I will also fight for family farms and ranches by pushing back on one-size-fits-all regulations and supporting reliable workers, affordable energy, and the ability to repair equipment. And I will focus on policies that help families and small businesses manage rising costs. Voters should consider my record of working across our communities as a county commissioner. I understand the challenges facing Central Washington because I have spent years listening to the people who live and work here. I will bring that experience to Congress and make sure our district’s voices are heard. We need a secure border and immigration laws that are enforced. That means stopping illegal crossings, disrupting fentanyl and human trafficking, and giving law enforcement the tools to do its job. We also need a legal immigration system that works. Agriculture and other employers in Central Washington depend on a reliable workforce. I support modernizing and streamlining the H-2A program so growers can find workers, workers are treated fairly, and farms have greater certainty from season to season. Border security and a workable legal process should go together. TSM; Explain why you support or reject the policies of the Democratic Socialist and progressive candidates around the country. I respect that voters are looking for solutions, but I disagree with policies that give the federal government more control over people’s lives, expand spending without a responsible plan to pay for it, and impose new costs on families, workers and small businesses. Government programs can have real consequences for the people who pay for them and the communities expected to follow one-size-fits-all rules. I believe we should focus on practical solutions: responsible budgeting, a strong economy, reliable energy, secure borders, and decisions made with local communities at the table. My approach is to protect individual freedom and opportunity while addressing real problems in ways that work for Central Washington. I do not support Medicare for All. I want to protect Medicare for seniors while preserving the ability of Americans to choose the coverage and doctors that work for them. A single government-run system could limit those choices and create major costs for taxpayers. We should work to make care more affordable by increasing competition, improving price transparency, and expanding options for small businesses and families. We also need to make sure people can get timely care close to home, including in rural communities. TSM; What are your keys to lowering consumer prices? We need to get federal spending under control, reduce unnecessary regulations, and make it easier to produce and move the goods families rely on. Reliable, affordable energy is part of that effort because higher energy costs affect nearly everything, from groceries to housing and transportation. I will also support policies that strengthen domestic agriculture, manufacturing, and supply chains and give small businesses room to grow. Central Washington families need practical steps that address the costs they face every day.

title: Taiwan Semiconductor Flexes Pricing Power on AI's Frontline - MarketBeat
content:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company NYSE: TSM sits just beneath that ceiling. Investors evaluating infrastructure plays might start to notice a shift in how value is captured across the silicon ecosystem. Industry reports suggest TSMC is preparing a coordinated series of price increases across its most advanced packaging and fabrication services, testing the limits of its pricing power. If implemented, those increases would help the foundry pass its expansion costs downstream. To build modern AI accelerators, designers integrate high-bandwidth memory directly alongside compute dies. This integration requires highly specialized advanced packaging. TSMC's proprietary Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate technology is the industry standard for this process, creating a commanding position in high-end AI packaging. Traditional organic substrates struggle to provide the fine-pitch interconnects necessary for the terabyte-per-second memory interfaces demanded by next-generation graphics processing units. When processing large language models, data transfer speed is just as critical as raw compute power, making silicon stacking a core requirement. Recognizing this heavy reliance, TSMC could raise prices for its advanced packaging services by 10% to 20%. Downstream clients like NVIDIA NASDAQ: NVDA and Advanced Micro Devices NASDAQ: AMD have little room to negotiate. This inability to negotiate stems from the fact that new architectures, such as NVIDIA's Blackwell and Rubin, require extensive testing cycles. According to industry estimates, final testing for Blackwell takes about four times as long as Hopper, while Rubin could require up to seven times as long as Hopper. These extended cycles lock up testing capacity and equipment bandwidth across the foundry. Fabless designers find themselves prioritizing guaranteed production slots over unit costs. Adding to the packaging premium, wafer prices for TSMC's advanced 2-nanometer and 3-nanometer nodes could increase by an estimated 3% to 6% starting in early 2027. Successfully implementing these rate hikes across service lines without causing client attrition would demonstrate the outsized leverage in the semiconductor space. Pricing power directly influences profitability, but those premiums are meant to help offset heavy capital requirements. In the third quarter of 2026, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company reported a slight sequential dip in gross margin, landing around 66.4%. At first glance, the contraction might suggest pricing weakness, but it reflects the capital-intensive ramp-up of the new 2-nanometer node. Advanced packaging margins, which have traditionally hovered below the corporate average, are steadily expanding toward parity as the new pricing structure takes effect. The foundry maintained its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to an estimated $60 billion-$64 billion. Upstream equipment lead times for specialized packaging tools have stretched to around six to eight months. To bypass these delays, management reportedly placed equipment orders at existing prices without negotiating its usual vendor discounts. They prioritize scale over immediate cost efficiency because they have the leverage to pass these higher capital expenditure requirements directly to customers. The strategy centers on ramping monthly advanced packaging capacity to roughly 130,000 wafers by the end of 2026, with an eye toward 200,000 wafers by 2027. Passing the expansion costs downstream allows TSMC to maintain an exceptional net margin, currently hovering near 51.5%, even while financing one of the largest industrial expansions in modern history. Beyond pricing leverage, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing exhibits stringent corporate discipline when navigating high-profile partnerships. Recent negotiations regarding Elon Musk's proposed Texas-based Terafab project highlight this dynamic. Despite the potential for a large influx of capital and guaranteed capacity demand, the foundry refused to yield operational control of the facility. As a result, Musk indicated that Tesla NASDAQ: TSLA and SpaceX NASDAQ: SPCX will build and run the facility themselves. By walking away from a joint venture that compromises internal standards, TSMC insulates itself from high-risk external capital expenditure projects. This decision protects the proprietary foundry moat and helps to keep management focused on high-margin, fully controlled operations rather than diluting expertise across experimental partnerships. Controlling the intellectual property and operational efficiency of every fab remains a core tenet of the underlying business model. Investors assessing the current landscape should consider how these fundamental shifts affect valuation. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing is trading with a forward price-to-earnings ratio of around 28. Given the raised revenue outlook, with recent quarterly revenue expanding over 41% year-over-year to approximately $46.72 billion and earnings per share beating estimates at $4.60, the market appears to be digesting the ability to command premium pricing. Interestingly, institutional investors currently own about 16.5% of TSMC stock, leaving substantial room for broader potential institutional buying as the advanced packaging narrative becomes more widely understood. Investors might want to weigh the broader macroeconomic impact of these supply chain premiums. As fabless designers absorb higher fabrication and packaging costs, inflationary pressure on silicon eventually trickles down to consumer hardware. Subsequent price increases in end-market products could dampen broader consumer-level aggregate demand over a multi-year horizon. Cautious investors may want to monitor downstream hardware sales data to gauge whether end consumers can absorb rising AI infrastructure costs, while those seeking exposure to the technology sector's physical backbone might add TSMC to their watchlist as its advanced-node expansion continues. TSM and MU have dipped 7% and 15.2%, respectively, so far this month, potentially offering investors an opportunity to gain exposure to the booming AI semiconductor market at more attractive prices. TSMC delivered third-quarter 2026 earnings of $4.60 per ADR, beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 3.4%, while revenues surged 41.2% year over year to $46.72 billion, surpassing estimates by 2.4%. Riding strong demand for advanced chips, particularly for AI applications, the company expects fourth-quarter revenues of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion, signaling continued momentum into year-end. Micron reported an impressive fiscal fourth-quarter 2026 performance, with adjusted EPS of $33.42 exceeding the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 5.73%. Revenues soared 379.3% year over year to $54.23 billion, beating estimates by 6.33%, as surging AI infrastructure investment fueled demand for memory products, including high-bandwidth memory (HBM). While both companies continue to benefit from substantial earnings growth and the expanding AI ecosystem, broader concerns about intensifying Chinese competition in the memory market, rising U.S. inflation and interest-rate expectations and the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending weigh on semiconductor stocks. Against this backdrop, the recent pullbacks in TSMC and Micron raise an important question — could this dip present a timely buying opportunity and which semiconductor stock should investors prioritize? Let's delve deeper. TSMC is positioned to benefit from sustained AI infrastructure investment. In the third quarter, revenues surged 41.2% year over year, while EPS per ADR rose 57.5%, exceeding expectations. High-performance computing revenue rose 22% sequentially and accounted for 68% of total revenues, while advanced technologies contributed 79% of wafer revenues. The outlook remains encouraging. TSMC expects fourth-quarter revenues of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion, implying approximately 58% year-over-year growth at the midpoint. Its financial position is also robust, with $126 billion in cash and marketable securities at quarter-end and approximately $28.8 billion in quarterly operating cash flow. However, gross margin declined sequentially from 67.7% to 66.4% as 2-nanometer production ramped up. Overseas fabrication facilities are another source of pressure, with management expecting their gross-margin impact to widen to 3–4 percentage points over the next few years. Micron's fiscal fourth-quarter 2026 results were strong, showing the earnings potential of the AI-driven memory market. Revenues soared to $54.23 billion from $11.32 billion a year earlier, while adjusted EPS reached $33.42, up from $3.03. Core Data Center revenue climbed to $18 billion from $1.58 billion a year earlier, reflecting surging demand for memory to support AI infrastructure. The company expects further acceleration in fiscal first-quarter 2027, forecasting revenues of $61.5 billion (+/- $1.5 billion) and adjusted EPS of $38.15 (+/- $1). This outlook indicates Micron's opportunity to capitalize on demand for high-bandwidth memory, server DRAM and other data-center products. Liquidity is another strength. Micron generated $43.97 billion in operating cash flow during the fourth quarter and ended fiscal 2026 with $73.48 billion in cash, marketable investments and restricted cash. However, the principal risks are the sustainability of exceptional memory pricing and earnings, the capital required to expand manufacturing capacity, and the cyclical nature of the memory industry. Micron's forecast of continued growth is encouraging, but it needs to be analyzed whether demand and pricing can sustain such elevated profitability as supply expands. TSMC trades at a forward 12-month P/E of 19.76, below its historical median of 21.14 and marginally above the Computer and Technology sector's 18.86. Micron appears significantly cheaper at 4.97X forward earnings versus its historical median of 10.07 and the sector's 18.86. At present, MU offers greater valuation appeal following its recent pullback, while TSMC trades closer to its historical median. However, Micron's unusually low multiple may reflect cyclical memory earnings and peak-profitability concerns. Both TSMC and Micron sport a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), reflecting favorable earnings estimate revisions following their strong quarterly results and upbeat outlooks. While MU appears more attractively valued based on its forward P/E, its earnings remain more exposed to memory pricing fluctuations and industry cyclicality. If investors had to choose just one, TSMC gets a marginal edge for its strong position in advanced chip manufacturing, diversified exposure to AI-driven demand across high-performance computing and other end markets and more established earnings visibility. Although margin pressures from advanced-node ramp-ups and overseas expansion warrant monitoring, TSMC offers a balance of AI-driven growth, competitive positioning and financial strength. Wei indicated that A14 customer engagement already exceeds comparable early N2 activity. Wei confirmed that TSMC is evaluating manufacturing expansion beyond Arizona, including potential opportunities in Texas. Responding to a JPMorgan analyst, Wei acknowledged discussions involving the proposed Terafab project. He clarified that any manufacturing collaboration would require TSMC operational control, although ownership arrangements remain under discussion. Meanwhile, Arizona's second fab is scheduled to begin 3-nanometer volume production in the third quarter of 2027. Huang expects overseas manufacturing to dilute gross margin by 3-4 percentage points during the latter portion of the company's five-year expansion period. Wei emphasized advanced packaging as another critical capacity priority amid increasing chip complexity and customer requirements. He reported successful production of five-reticle-size packaging solutions, with development progressing toward nine- and 14-reticle-size configurations. He identified CoWoS as customers' preferred packaging solution. During the Q&A, Wei also discussed collaboration with GlobalFoundries to support interposer supply. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company TSM is one of, if not the most important companies in the world, making it a nearly surefire long-term investment in artificial intelligence and technology in general. Taiwan Semi, or TSMC, physically manufactures the most cutting-edge semiconductors fueling the artificial intelligence boom and the wider tech-driven economy. The chip builder reported a strong beat-and-raise Q3 on October 15, confirming that the AI capex spending spree remains full-steam ahead even as bubble concerns ramp up. The chart below showcases Taiwan Semi's impressive earnings expansion, including ~400% growth between 2019 and 2025. TSMC's Q4 earnings estimate surged ~12% since its mid-month release, while its FY27 estimate jumped significantly as well to help it earn a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy). Its robust guidance is supported by "continued strong demand" for its "leading-edge process technologies, including the steep ramp-up of our 2-nanometer technology." The stock, which nearly quadrupled the Tech sector over the last 15 years and tripled it over the past five, is down ~12% from its recent peaks. TSMC is on the verge of a possible technical breakout, and it is trading at a 43% discount to its highs and in line with its 10-year median at 19.5X forward earnings. AI and the global economy rely, directly or indirectly, on semiconductors. More importantly, TSMC likely manufactured a large share of the chips fueling the AI boom and beyond, since the chip builder reportedly captures 60% of the foundry market and 90% of advanced semiconductor manufacturing. The company on a tiny island doesn't design or sell its own semiconductors. Instead, TSMC was founded in the late 1980s on a simple, yet revolutionary "pure-play foundry" model, dedicated exclusively to manufacturing advanced semiconductors for other tech companies. Taiwan Semi has built an almost unbreachable fortress around its leading-edge chip-building business by earning the trust of customers such as Nvidia (NVDA), Apple (AAPL), AMD, Qualcomm, and other tech titans. Nvidia, Apple, and others rely on TSMC because of its unmatched scale and expertise. Plus, their CEOs know that Taiwan Semi is their partner, not a competitor. The company is also critically rushing to expand its global manufacturing operation outside of Taiwan into the U.S., Japan, and beyond to address one of its only potential shortfalls: geopolitics. Wall Street is still waiting for Amazon, Alphabet, Nvidia, and many other tech firms to report third-quarter earnings. But TSMC already confirmed that the AI capital spending boom is ramping up. TSM grew its Q3 earnings by 58% on 41% higher revenue. The chip builder said that 3- nanometer shipments accounted for 33% of its total wafer revenue, up from 23% in the year-ago period. Plus, its most advanced 2-nm chips accounted for 8%, up from 3% in the second quarter (first time 2-nm shipments were broken out in its earnings release). TSMC's Q4 earnings estimate surged 12% since its Q3 release on October 15, with its fiscal 2027 estimate 6% higher. The recent positivity extends its impressive run of upward earnings revisions, and its most accurate estimates for FY26 and FY27 came in above consensus. The tech giant's overall upbeat earnings revisions land it a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) right now. The leading chip builder said at the start of 2026 that it expects to grow its revenue by a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of ~25% between 2024 and 2029. TSMC is projected to grow its revenue by 41% in 2026 and another 33% next year to reach $229 billion, adding more than $100 billion vs. 2025's $122 billion total and more than tripling its 2023 figure. On the bottom line, it's projected to grow its earnings by 60% in 2026 and 32% next year, more than doubling its 2025 total ($10.65) in the process ($22.44 a share in 2027). TSMC's robust guidance is supported by "continued strong demand" for its "leading-edge process technologies, including the steep ramp-up of our 2-nanometer technology." The chip builder is nearly neck-and-neck with Nvidia over the last three years, skyrocketing ~400%, while leaving the rest of the Mag 7 in the dust. TSM is down roughly 12% from its October 5 records, and its average Zacks price target implies 27% upside from Monday's levels. title: Nvidia, Chipmakers Face Higher Costs? TSMC Reportedly Plans Up To 20% Price Hike For Advanced Chip Packaging - TradingView
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSM) is preparing to raise prices for its advanced packaging process by 10%-20% as surging demand for AI chips strains production capacity, Taiwan’s China Times reported on Tuesday, citing supply-chain sources. If it goes through with the plan, it would raise costs for several chip firms, including Nvidia Corp (NVDA) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD). The move could also put further pressure on the prices of Apple’s (AAPL) iPhones and MacBooks, which have already seen price increases amid rising memory chip costs. TSMC is considering raising prices for CoWoS (Chip on Wafer on Substrate), its advanced packaging technology that integrates chips and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) into a single package. The report says the potential hike is being considered as demand for advanced packaging expands beyond GPUs to server CPUs and custom AI chips or ASICs, leading to capacity constraints. TSMC is continuing to ramp up its advanced packaging operations to meet demand, with monthly CoWoS capacity expected to exceed 130,000 units in 2026 and 200,000 units next year, China Times reported. TSMC is the world’s largest contract chipmaker, making advanced chips that power everything from AI data centers to smartphones. Its major customers also include Broadcom, Qualcomm and MediaTek. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment was ‘bullish’ for NVDA and AMD, and ‘bearish’ for TSM. TSM stock hit a record high on Oct. 5 but has since been caught up in the selloff in AI-linked stocks amid renewed concerns about the sustainability and returns of massive AI investments. Shares remain 40.5% up year to date. NVDA has declined about 11% from its record close on Oct. 6, but it has been up 16% year-to-date. “$CRWV $NVDA $TSM Ignore the noise from Musk. He's scared,” said a trader, referring to the SpaceX CEO’s bearish comments on the neocloud sector, which pressured several cloud and AI-linked stocks on Monday.
